latin.2528: XC. Porro quum Doctor iste dicit, si duobus hominibus aequalia auxilia ex parte Dei dentur, fieri posse ut unus pro sua libertate convertatur, & alter non: monet id se intelligere de auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, qua praeveniens est. Nam si agatur de gratiae ejusdem auxiliis, quatenus est cooperans, id est, quatenus per eam Deus influit in actum quem homo libere elicit, non amplius verum est, aequali auxilio dato, unum converti, alterum non converti. Siquidem impossibile est aliquem non converti, & tamen Deum in eo efficere, cum libero ejus arbitrio, conversionis actum. Sed quoniam gratia praeveniens & cooperans reapse sunt unum & idem, & gratiae cooperatio a liberi nostri arbitrii cooperatione pendet, non secus ac concursus & influxus cujusvis habitus, ab operatione potentiae cui inest: simpliciter & absolute loquendo dicendum putat, unum cum aequalibus, aut etiam cum minoribus auxiliis pro sua libertate converti, ac salvari, quando alius neque convertitur neque salvatur. Licet si in summo rigore loquamur, dici non debeat cum aequalibus gratiae auxiliis unum converti, alterum non converti: quoniam in eo qui convertitur est influxus quidam gratiae, qui in alio non est; ille nimirum qui pendet a liberi nostri arbitrii consensu.
latin.2529: XCI. Similiter juxta hunc Doctorem affirmandum non est, existentibus in duobus adultis aequalibus auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, illum qui convertitur, pro sola sua libertate converti. Quoniam licet conversio illa a libertate pendeat, fiatque ab arbitrio pro sua libertate; non tamen fit pro sola sua libertate, sed cooperante simul auxilio gratiae praevenientis per influxum a quo sortitur rationem gratiae cooperantis: quamvis cum hic praesto sit, gratiamque praevenientem dependenter a cooperatione arbitrii comitetur, solum exigatur cooperatio libera arbitrii nostri. Disputatione quadragesima ad articulum 13. quaestionis 14. paragr. ad secundam.
latin.2530: XCII. Inde vero sequitur, juxta illius hypotheses, positis quibusvis auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, qua praeveniens est, hominem posse non converti, tam in sensu composito, quam in sensu diviso. At posito ejusdem gratiae auxilio, quatenus est cooperans, hominem posse quidem non converti in sensu diviso; Verum id falsum esse in sensu composito; quia fieri non potest, ut adsit influxus gratiae cooperantis, quatenus est cooperans conversionem, quin peccator per suum arbitrium convertatur; quod tamen arbitrii libertati nihil officit: quia influxus iste gratiae cooperantis, ab arbitrii humani consensu, ut saepe jam dictum est, pendet. Ut videre est in eadem disputatione paragr. hinc patet.
latin.2531: XCIII. Quae sit autem natura divinae illius gratiae, quae diverso respectu praeveniens & cooperans est, & quam liberum hominis arbitrium efficacem vel inefficacem reddit, prolixe explicat Molina disputatione 45. ad articulum 13. quaestionis 14. Et primo quidem in genere gratiam illam constituit in mentis quadam illuminatione, & in motibus quibusdam voluntatis.
latin.2532: XCIV. Ista vero mentis illuminatio ipsi nihil est aliud, quam notitiae quaedam ab externo concionatore, aut aliunde acceptae, & a Deo peculiari, & supernaturali influxu adjutae, ut aliquo modo jam ad salutem accommodatae sint. Observat enim Deum illis quos ordinaria ratione illuminat, non immittere novas species & ideas, quibus fiant cognitiones illae, quarum interventu mens eorum illustratur; sed cognitiones illas fieri per species humano modo acquisitas, & a concionatoribus, aut alia aliqua ratione excitatas, quibus Deus se inserit per suum influxum, ut cognitiones istae ad salutem plus minus accommodatae fiant, pro ratione majoris, vel minoris influxus. Quare, ex ejus sententia, Deum illuminare non aliud est, quam illo modo influxu suo cooperari ad tales cognitiones quibus voluntas excitatur.
latin.2533: XCV. Motus vero voluntatis, in quibus gratia praeveniens consistit, ex illius mente, sunt certi quidam affectus, quibus praevia cognitione, voluntas erigitur, & invitatur, tum ad eliciendam spem, tum ad diligendum Deum, aut dolendum de peccatis, antequam actum spei, aut amoris, vel doloris ex dilectione ejus eliciat. Ad hujusmodi vero motus & affectus non cooperatur voluntas, qua liberum arbitrium est, sed solum qua voluntas, & natura quaedam est. Quippe velit nolit, praesente cognitione, naturaliter in ea insurgunt. Rationem autem gratiae non habent, nisi Deus simul in eosdem specialiter influat, ut evadant supernaturales, & certo quoque modo ad salutem accommodentur.
latin.2534: XCVI. Quod ut plenius intelligi possit, observat ex contemplatione rei valde amabilis, & quam multum refert adipisci, naturaliter consurgere in voluntate motum quendam, quo voluntas ad illam afficitur: qui motus non est volitio, sed affectio voluntatis ad illam rem, a cujus bonitate quasi tangitur & allicitur ad volendum eam. Atque hic motus, juxta ipsum, volitionem antecedere solet, non tantum in hominibus, sed etiam in angelis; idque tam in statu naturae integrae, quam in statu naturae corruptae. Quoniam prius tempore, vel natura fuit Luciferum ad id affici voluntate, quod per superbiam obtinere voluit, quam illud libere vellet. Sicut prius etiam fuit, Evam affici ad pomum vetitum, quam illud comedere vellet contra legem Dei.
latin.2535: XCVII. Porro post ejusmodi motum in voluntate ex rei contemplatione exortum, in voluntatis potestate situm est, rem simpliciter velle vel non velle. Sed motus iste, quo ad rem afficitur, non libere, ut jam dictum, sed mere naturaliter in voluntate oritur, posita rei contemplatione. Voluntas tamen indirecte potest hujusmodi motum in se impedire, arcendo nempe cogitationem, & divertendo ad alia, ac procurando ut mens voluntati alia proponat, quae eam ad omnino contraria allicere solent.
latin.2536: XCVIII. Quod si existente affectu ad aliquam rem, quam mens ut amabilem concipit, & voluntati offert, menti occurrat via & aditus, quo obtineri posse credatur, naturaliter etiam consurgit in voluntate motus quidam quasi erectionis illius ad sperandum, qui tempore, vel natura, antecedit actum liberum spei. Adeoque motus ille a notitia bonitatis objecti, & notitia viae qua obtineri posse creditur, cooperante voluntate, non ut libera, sed natura quaedam est, efficitur; exurgitque naturaliter in voluntate, eo major, quo notitia bonitatis objecti, & viae qua obtineri possit, major & verisimilior est, sicuti se res habet in affectu illo voluntatis ad objectum cognitum simpliciter ut bonum.
latin.2537: XCIX. Jam autem Doctor ille non aliud gratiae tribuit quam ut perficiat naturam, eamque adjuvet in suis motibus, ut unusquisque ex supernaturali auxilio & gratia talis sit, qualis ad salutem oportet. Ac proinde ad dignoscendos & explicandos motus gratiae, vult attendi ad progressum & ordinem, quem natura ipsa, potentiaeve cognoscentes & appetentes servarent, si illos eosdem actus, qui gratiae tribuuntur, suis solis viribus quoad substantiam actus producerent, quod fieri posse ille existimat. Ut ea ratione intelligatur quo pacto Deus per auxilia ac dona gratiae, se inserat & cooperetur cum natura, eamque adjuvet, ut supra suas vires eos actus producat quales ad salutem necessarii sunt.
latin.2538: C. Itaque motus illos in quibus constituit gratiam praevenientem, censet esse operationes vitales, a facultatibus nostris active procedentes, sed quae tamen libere ab eis non eliciuntur, nec dici debent actus liberi arbitrii, proprie loquendo, quanquam multum a libero arbitrio pendeant. Idque quoniam liberum arbitrium variis modis potest actus illos juvare, vel impedire, eosque desiderare & petere a Deo, & quodammodo seipsum aptare & disponere, ut juxta communem cursum & ordinem divinae providentiae, facilius sibi a Deo donentur.
latin.2539: CI. Exempli gratia, notitiae illae rerum credendarum, quibus accedente quodam influxu supernaturali, mens nostra salutariter illustrari incipit, libere comparari possunt, aurem praebendo concionatoribus, & libros pios evolvendo, aliave simili quapiam ratione: ut & ab eis potest aliquis sese libere avertere, & ita divinae illuminationi obstaculum ponere: Licet notitiae illae rationem gratiae praevenientis obtineant, solum ab influxu Dei supernaturali, non vero a libero hominis arbitrio. Et eodem modo pii illi affectus, qui posita Dei illuminatione, naturaliter & necessario in voluntate resultant, & qui rationem habent gratiae praevenientis, ex parte voluntatis, si peculiaris quidam Dei influxus ad eos accedat, possunt a libero hominis arbitrio impediri, dum homo libere cessat a pia cogitatione, aut adducit & quaerit rationes allicientes voluntatem in partem oppositam; & contra juvari, si quis mentem ultro retineat in pia illa cogitatione.
latin.2540: CII. Sed ut clarius pateat quae sit Molinae sententia, non alienum erit verbis ipsius exponere ordinem & rationem motuum gratiae praevenientis, qua vocamur ad fidem, spem, dilectionem, & contritionem, quibus hominis conversio constat. Sic ergo jam dicta disputatione ea de re philosophatur. Dum homo, inquit, nondum ad fidem supernaturaliter interius vocatus, cogitat & expendit res credendas, per notitias concionatoris ministerio, aut aliunde comparatas, influit Deus in easdem notitias influxu quodam particulari ac supernaturali, quo cognitionem illam adjuvat, tum ut res melius & dilucidius expendatur, & penetretur, tum etiam ut notitia illa jam limites notitiae supernaturalis, & ad finem supernaturalem in suo ordine & gradu accommodatae attingat. Ex cognitione vero & penetratione earum rerum quae ad fidem spectant, nempe quum expenditur quam digne sint quibus assensus adhibeatur, quantumque id expediat, oritur naturaliter in voluntate motus affectionis ad res ita cognitas, quo allicitur, & quasi invitatur, ad imperandum intellectui assensum, quo eis assentiatur. Cum hoc ergo motu quasi se inserit etiam Deus; influens in illum per auxilium particulare, illumque eo auxilio quasi acuit, ut magis urgeat & alliciat, efficitque illum supernaturalem, ut in suo ordine & gradu sit etiam ad salutem accommodatus.
latin.2541: CIII. Porro liberum arbitrium his duobus motibus gratiae praevenientis adjutum & excitatum, liberam adhuc habet potestatem imperandi, aut non imperandi assensum fidei. Quod si voluntas fidem amplecti velit, actumque credendi imperet intellectui, influente simul motu gratiae praevenientis, quam habet, elicit in seipsa actum supernaturalem, quo fidem amplecti vult, quoque assensum imperat intellectui: simulque intellectus motus imperio illo supernaturali voluntatis, illustrationeque divina adjutus, elicit actum supernaturalem assentiendi revelatis, hisque duobus actibus supernaturalibus intellectus & voluntatis homo rite dispositus suscipit habitum fidei supernaturalem, a Deo solo infusum, quo deinceps similes actus supernaturales valeat producere.
latin.2542: CIV. Quod spectat gratiae motum, quo ad spei actum excitamur, sic mentem suam de illo explicat. Dum intellectus, inquit, illustratus jam lumine fidei supernaturalis, sempiternam beatitudinem homini a Deo praeparatam cogitat, bonitatem ac excellentiam illius, tum multa alia & praeclara Dei opera, ac beneficia in hominem collata, de quorum numero sunt Christi incarnatio ac passio, consideratque reliqua media quae sibi ad vitam aeternam consequendam abundantissime suppeditata sunt, naturaliter oritur in voluntate non solum affectus ad beatitudinem, quo allicitur & invitatur ut eam amore concupiscentiae velit, sed etiam motus erectionis, quo attrahitur & allicitur ad eam ipsam a Deo sperandam. Quamvis autem hic motus a libero arbitrio pendeat, si a cogitatione ex qua motus oritur cesset; nihilominus sublatis impedimentis, mere naturaliter insurgit, eique quasi se ingerit Deus specialiter influendo, eumque acuit & efficit supernaturalem, ut in suo ordine & gradu sit qualis ad salutem necessarius est; per eumque supernaturaliter erigit, & quasi invitat voluntatem, ut eliciat actum supernaturalem sperandi sempiternam beatitudinem, & media ad illam comparandam necessaria. Per ejusmodi ergo gratiam liberum nostrum arbitrium, a Deo praeventum & excitatum elicit, si vult, primum actum spei supernaturalis liberum, quo rite dispositum consequitur a Deo habitum spei supernaturalis, per quem in posterum elicere possit alios similes actus supernaturales quotiescunque voluerit.
latin.2543: CV. Quibus consentanea quoque circa gratiam ad actum Dilectionis Dei, & contritionis de peccatis necessariam edisserit. Deinde, inquit, quum intellectus lumine fidei illustratus, praeexistenteque actu spei supernaturalis in voluntate, Dei bonitatem tum secundum se, tum erga nos considerat, & tam multa ac magna beneficia quibus tam suaviter nos praevenit, naturaliter excitatur in voluntate motio amoris amicitiae erga Deum quo ea potentia allicitur, & ad Deum diligendum invitatur. Huic etiam motui se inserit Deus, illumque suo supernaturali influxu, non solum acuit & incendit, sed etiam efficit supernaturalem, qualis videlicet, in suo ordine & gradu est ad salutem necessarius.
latin.2544: CVI. Quod si simul accedat cognitio magnitudinis, multitudinis, atque ingratitudinis peccatorum, quibus Deum offendimus, liberum arbitrium gratia eadem praeventum, ut elicere potest actum dilectionis Dei supernaturalis, ita poterit elicere actum veri doloris de peccatis, propter Deum ex affectu amoris supernaturalis dilectum, qui est vera contritio, & ultima dispositio ad gratiam gratum facientem, quae in eodem instanti, posterius tamen natura, contritionem ipsam consequitur.
latin.2545: CVII. Caeterum autor ille distinguit inter auxilium gratiae praevenientis, & inter gratiam ipsam praevenientem. Et quidem per gratiam praevenientem intelligit illas cognitiones mentis, & affectiones voluntatis, quas Deus influxu quodam particulari acuit & adjuvat, ut fiant supernaturales; & in gradu & ordine suo, quales ad salutem oportet. Per auxilium vero gratiae praevenientis intelligit influxum illum supernaturalem, quo Deus cognitiones istas, humana ut plurimum ratione acquisitas, & affectiones, posita ejusmodi cognitione mere naturaliter in voluntate insurgentes, quo modo dictum est, acuit, adjuvat & incendit, ut evadant supernaturales, & quales ad aeternam hominis salutem conducit.

sections.title: Equal aids: true of prevenient grace, not of cooperating grace
sections.pass_a: XC. Moreover when that Doctor says, if equal aids be given to two men on the part of God, it can come about that one by his liberty is converted, & the other not: he warns that he understands this of the aids of prevenient grace, as it is prevenient. For if it be a question of the aids of the same grace, as far as it is cooperating, that is, as far as through it God flows into the act which man freely elicits, it is no longer true, equal aid being given, that one is converted, the other not converted. Since it is impossible that someone be not converted, & yet that God effect in him, with his free choice, the act of conversion. But since prevenient & cooperating grace are really one & the same, & the cooperation of grace depends on the cooperation of our free choice, not otherwise than the concurrence & influx of any habit, on the operation of the power in which it is: simply & absolutely speaking he thinks it must be said, that one with equal, or even with lesser aids by his liberty is converted, and saved, when another is neither converted nor saved. Although if we speak in the highest rigour, it ought not to be said that with equal aids of grace one is converted, the other not converted: since in him who is converted there is a certain influx of grace, which in the other is not; namely that which depends on the consent of our free choice.
pass_b: Thesis XC. When Molina says that if God gives two people equal aids, one may be converted by his own freedom and the other not, he warns that he means the aids of prevenient grace, taken as prevenient. If we speak of that same grace as cooperating, that is, as the grace through which God flows into the act a person freely elicits, it is no longer true that with equal aid one is converted and the other is not. It is impossible for someone not to be converted while God is nevertheless producing in him, together with his free choice, the act of conversion.

Yet prevenient and cooperating grace are in reality one and the same, and the cooperation of grace depends on the cooperation of our free choice, just as the concurrence and influence of any habit depends on the working of the power it resides in. So, speaking simply and absolutely, he thinks one must say that a person is converted and saved by his freedom with equal or even smaller aids, while another is neither converted nor saved. Speaking with the utmost strictness, though, one should not say that with equal aids of grace one is converted and the other not, since in the one converted there is an influence of grace not present in the other: the influence that depends on the consent of our free choice.

sections.title: Not converted by freedom alone
sections.pass_a: XCI. Likewise according to this Doctor it is not to be affirmed, equal aids of prevenient grace existing in two adults, that he who is converted, is converted by his liberty alone. Since although that conversion depends on liberty, and comes about from choice by its liberty; yet it does not come about by its liberty alone, but with the aid of prevenient grace cooperating at the same time through an influx from which it obtains the character of cooperating grace: although when this is at hand, and accompanies prevenient grace dependently on the cooperation of choice, only the free cooperation of our choice is required. Disputation forty on article 13. of question 14. paragraph on the second.
pass_b: Thesis XCI. In the same way, according to this Doctor, one must not say that when two adults have equal aids of prevenient grace, the one who is converted is converted by his freedom alone. That conversion does depend on freedom and is brought about by choice in its freedom. But it is not brought about by that freedom alone: the aid of prevenient grace cooperates with it at the same time, through the influence by which it takes on the character of cooperating grace.

Even so, when that influence is present and accompanies prevenient grace in dependence on the cooperation of choice, nothing more is required than the free cooperation of our choice. This is in disputation 40 on article 13 of question 14, in the paragraph 'Ad secundam'.

sections.title: Able not to be converted: composite and divided sense
sections.pass_a: XCII. Hence indeed it follows, according to his hypotheses, any aids whatever of prevenient grace being posited, as it is prevenient, that man can not be converted, as well in the composite sense, as in the divided sense. But the aid of the same grace being posited, as far as it is cooperating, that man can indeed not be converted in the divided sense; But that this is false in the composite sense; because it cannot come about, that the influx of cooperating grace be present, as far as it is cooperating in conversion, but that the sinner be converted by his choice; which yet hinders nothing to the liberty of choice: because that influx of cooperating grace, depends on the consent of human choice, as has often now been said. As is to be seen in the same disputation paragr. hence it is clear.
pass_b: Thesis XCII. It follows from his assumptions that, whatever aids of prevenient grace are given, taken as prevenient, a person is able not to be converted, in the composite sense as well as in the divided sense. Given the aid of the same grace as cooperating, however, a person can indeed fail to be converted in the divided sense, but not in the composite sense.

For the influence of cooperating grace cannot be present, as cooperating in conversion, without the sinner being converted through his own choice. This takes nothing away from the freedom of choice, because, as has been said many times already, that influence of cooperating grace depends on the consent of human choice. This can be seen in the same disputation, in the paragraph beginning 'Hinc patet'.

sections.title: Molina's account of the nature of grace: illumination and motions
sections.pass_a: XCIII. But what the nature of that divine grace is, which in different respect is prevenient & cooperating, & which the free choice of man renders efficacious or inefficacious, Molina explains at length in disputation 45. on article 13. of question 14. And first indeed in general he places that grace in a certain illumination of the mind, & in certain motions of the will.
pass_b: Thesis XCIII. Molina explains at length, in disputation 45 on article 13 of question 14, the nature of this divine grace, which is prevenient in one respect and cooperating in another, and which man's free choice makes efficacious or inefficacious. To begin with, he places that grace in general in an illumination of the mind and in certain motions of the will.

sections.title: Illumination: acquired knowledge helped by God's influence
sections.pass_a: XCIV. That illumination of the mind is to him nothing other, than certain notions received from an external preacher, or from elsewhere, & helped by God's peculiar & supernatural influx, so that in some manner they are now accommodated to salvation. For he observes that God does not send into those whom he illuminates in the ordinary way new species & ideas, by which those cognitions come about, by whose intervention their mind is enlightened; but that those cognitions come about through species acquired in human manner, & excited by preachers, or in some other way, into which God inserts himself by his influx, that those cognitions may become more or less accommodated to salvation, according to the measure of the greater, or lesser influx. Wherefore, in his opinion, for God to illuminate is nothing other, than in that manner by his influx to cooperate in such cognitions by which the will is excited.
pass_b: Thesis XCIV. For him this illumination of the mind is simply a set of notions received from an external preacher or from some other source, and helped by a special, supernatural influence of God so that they are in some way already fitted for salvation. He observes that when God enlightens people in the ordinary way he does not send into them new species and ideas from which that knowledge arises, the knowledge through whose intervention their minds are enlightened.

That knowledge arises through species acquired in the human way and stirred up by preachers or by some other means. God inserts himself into them by his influence, so that this knowledge becomes more or less fitted for salvation, in proportion as his influence is greater or smaller. On Molina's view, then, for God to enlighten is nothing else than to cooperate in this way, by his influence, in the kinds of knowledge that rouse the will.

sections.title: The motions of the will in prevenient grace arise naturally
sections.pass_a: XCV. But the motions of the will, in which prevenient grace consists, according to his mind, are certain affections, by which, cognition going before, the will is raised, & invited, both to eliciting hope, and to loving God, or grieving for sins, before it elicits the act of hope, or of love, or of grief from love of him. But to motions & affections of this kind the will does not cooperate, as it is free choice, but only as it is will, & a certain nature. Since whether it will or not, cognition being present, they rise up naturally in it. But they do not have the character of grace, unless God at the same time flows specially into them, that they become supernatural, & also in a certain manner be accommodated to salvation.
pass_b: Thesis XCV. On his view the motions of the will that make up prevenient grace are certain affections. Once knowledge has gone before, they raise and invite the will to elicit hope, to love God or to grieve for sins, before it elicits the act of hope, or of love, or of grief arising from love of him.

The will does not cooperate in these motions and affections as free choice, but only as will, that is, as a kind of nature. Whether it wants them or not, they rise up in it naturally once the knowledge is present. They have the character of grace only if God at the same time flows specially into them, so that they become supernatural and are also fitted in a certain way for salvation.

sections.title: The natural motion that precedes volition: Lucifer and Eve
sections.pass_a: XCVI. That this may be understood more fully, he observes that from the contemplation of a thing very lovable, & which it matters much to obtain, there naturally rises in the will a certain motion, by which the will is affected toward it: which motion is not volition, but an affection of the will toward that thing, by whose goodness it is as it were touched & allured to will it. And this motion, according to him, is wont to precede volition, not only in men, but also in angels; and that as well in the state of nature integral, as in the state of nature corrupt. Since it was earlier in time, or nature, that Lucifer was affected in will toward that, which he willed to obtain through pride, than that he freely willed it. As it was also earlier, that Eve was affected toward the forbidden apple, than that she willed to eat it against the law of God.
pass_b: Thesis XCVI. To make this clearer, he observes that when we contemplate something very lovable and well worth obtaining, a motion rises naturally in the will by which it is drawn toward that thing. This motion is not a volition. It is an affection of the will toward the thing, whose goodness, so to speak, touches it and entices it to will it.

According to Molina this motion normally comes before volition, in angels as well as in men, and in the state of intact nature as well as in that of fallen nature. Lucifer's will was drawn toward what he sought to gain through pride before, in time or in nature, he freely willed it. In the same way Eve was drawn toward the forbidden fruit before she willed to eat it against God's law.

sections.title: The will can hinder this motion only indirectly
sections.pass_a: XCVII. Moreover after such a motion has arisen in the will from the contemplation of the thing, it is placed in the will's power, simply to will the thing or not to will it. But that motion, by which it is affected toward the thing, arises in the will not freely, as has now been said, but merely naturally, the contemplation of the thing being posited. The will however can indirectly hinder such a motion in itself, namely by warding off the thought, & by turning aside to other things, and by procuring that the mind propose other things to the will, which are wont to allure it to things wholly contrary.
pass_b: Thesis XCVII. Once such a motion has arisen in the will from contemplating the thing, it is in the will's power simply to will the thing or not to will it. The motion by which the will is drawn toward the thing, however, does not arise freely, as was said; it arises in the will purely by nature once the thing is contemplated.

Still, the will can hinder that motion in itself indirectly: by keeping the thought away, by turning to other matters, and by seeing to it that the mind sets before the will other things that usually draw it toward the very opposite.

sections.title: The natural motion toward hope
sections.pass_a: XCVIII. But if, an affection existing toward some thing, which the mind conceives as lovable, & offers to the will, there occurs to the mind a way & access, by which it is believed it can be obtained, there also naturally rises in the will a certain motion as it were of its uplifting toward hoping, which in time, or nature, precedes the free act of hope. And so that motion is effected by the knowledge of the goodness of the object, & the knowledge of the way by which it is believed it can be obtained, the will cooperating, not as free, but as it is a certain nature; and it rises up naturally in the will, the greater, the greater & more probable is the knowledge of the goodness of the object, & of the way by which it can be obtained, just as the matter stands in that affection of the will toward the object known simply as good.
pass_b: Thesis XCVIII. Suppose there is an affection toward something that the mind conceives as lovable and presents to the will, and the mind then sees a way and an approach by which it believes the thing can be obtained. A motion then also rises naturally in the will, a kind of uplift toward hoping, which comes before the free act of hope in time or in nature.

That motion is produced by the knowledge of the object's goodness and the knowledge of the way it is believed it can be obtained, with the will cooperating not as free but as a kind of nature. It rises naturally in the will, and it is the stronger, the greater and more probable is the knowledge of the object's goodness and of the way to obtain it. The same holds for the will's affection toward an object known simply as good.

sections.title: Grace only perfects and helps nature
sections.pass_a: XCIX. Now that Doctor attributes nothing else to grace than that it perfect nature, and help it in its motions, so that each one from supernatural aid & grace be such, as is needful for salvation. And therefore for discerning & explaining the motions of grace, he wants attention paid to the progress & order, which nature itself, or the knowing & appetitive powers would keep, if they produced those same acts, which are attributed to grace, by their own forces alone as to the substance of the act, which he thinks can be done. That in that way it may be understood how God through the aids and gifts of grace, inserts himself & cooperates with nature, and helps it, that above its forces it produce those acts such as are necessary for salvation.
pass_b: Thesis XCIX. Molina gives grace no other role than to perfect nature and help it in its own motions, so that each person becomes, through supernatural aid and grace, what salvation requires. To identify and explain the motions of grace, therefore, he wants us to look at the course and order that nature itself, or the knowing and desiring powers, would follow if they produced, by their own strength alone, the substance of the same acts that are attributed to grace. He thinks this can happen.

In this way we are to understand how God, through the aids and gifts of grace, inserts himself into nature, cooperates with it and helps it, so that it produces beyond its own strength such acts as are necessary for salvation.

sections.title: Prevenient motions are vital operations, not free acts
sections.pass_a: C. Therefore those motions in which he places prevenient grace, he thinks are vital operations, proceeding actively from our faculties, but which yet are not freely elicited by them, nor ought to be called acts of free choice, properly speaking, although they depend much on free choice. And that because free choice can in various ways help those acts, or hinder them, and desire and ask them from God, & in a certain way fit & dispose itself, that according to the common course & order of divine providence, they be more easily given it by God.
pass_b: Thesis C. So he holds that the motions in which he places prevenient grace are vital operations proceeding actively from our faculties. Yet they are not elicited freely by those faculties, and strictly speaking they should not be called acts of free choice, though they depend a great deal on free choice.

The reason is that free choice can help or hinder those acts in various ways, can desire them and ask God for them, and can in some way fit and dispose itself so that, by the common course and order of divine providence, they may be given to it by God more readily.

sections.title: How free choice helps or hinders prevenient grace
sections.pass_a: CI. For example, those notions of things to be believed, by which, a certain supernatural influx being added, our mind begins to be illuminated salutarily, can be freely procured, by lending the ear to preachers, & by turning over pious books, or in some other similar way: as also a person can freely turn himself away from them, & so put an obstacle to divine illumination: Although those notions obtain the character of prevenient grace, only from God's supernatural influx, not from man's free choice. And in the same way those pious affections, which, God's illumination being posited, result naturally & necessarily in the will, & which have the character of prevenient grace, on the part of the will, if a certain peculiar influx of God be added to them, can be hindered by man's free choice, while a man freely ceases from pious thought, or brings forward & seeks reasons alluring the will to the opposite side; & on the contrary be helped, if one of his own accord keeps the mind in that pious thought.
pass_b: Thesis CI. For example, the notions of things to be believed, through which, with a supernatural influence added, our mind begins to be enlightened for salvation, can be acquired freely: by listening to preachers, by reading devout books, or in some similar way. Equally, a person can freely turn away from them and so put an obstacle in the way of God's illumination. Even so, those notions get the character of prevenient grace only from God's supernatural influence, not from man's free choice.

The same is true of the devout affections that result naturally and necessarily in the will once God's illumination is given, and that have the character of prevenient grace on the will's side if some special influence of God is added to them. Man's free choice can hinder them, when he freely stops thinking devout thoughts or brings up and looks for reasons that draw the will the other way. It can also help them, when someone of his own accord keeps his mind fixed on that devout thought.

sections.title: Molina in his own words: the motions of prevenient grace toward faith
sections.pass_a: CII. But that it may appear more clearly what Molina's opinion is, it will not be foreign to set out in his own words the order & manner of the motions of prevenient grace, by which we are called to faith, hope, love, & contrition, of which man's conversion consists. Thus then in the disputation already mentioned he philosophizes on that matter. While a man, he says, not yet called inwardly in a supernatural way to faith, thinks over & weighs the things to be believed, through notions procured by the ministry of a preacher, or from elsewhere, God flows into those same notions by a certain particular & supernatural influx, by which he helps that cognition, both that the thing be weighed better & more clearly, & penetrated, and also that that notion may now attain the limits of a supernatural notion, & one accommodated in its order & degree to a supernatural end. But from the cognition & penetration of those things that pertain to faith, namely when it is weighed how worthy they are that assent be given them, & how much it is expedient, there arises naturally in the will a motion of affection toward the things so known, by which it is allured, & as it were invited, to command the intellect's assent, by which it may assent to them. With this motion then God also as it were inserts himself; flowing into it through a particular aid, and by that aid as it were sharpens it, that it may urge & allure more, and makes it supernatural, that in its order & degree it be also accommodated to salvation.
pass_b: Thesis CII. To show Molina's view more clearly, it will be to the point to set out in his own words the order and pattern of the motions of prevenient grace by which we are called to faith, hope, love and contrition, in which a person's conversion consists. In the disputation already cited he reasons about this as follows.

'While a person not yet inwardly called to faith in a supernatural way thinks over and weighs the things to be believed, through notions acquired by a preacher's ministry or from some other source,' he says, 'God flows into those notions by a particular, supernatural influence. By it he helps that knowledge, so that the matter is weighed better and more clearly and is penetrated, and also so that the knowledge now reaches the level of supernatural knowledge, fitted in its order and degree to a supernatural end.

When the mind weighs and enters into the things that belong to faith, that is, how worthy they are of assent and how much it matters to assent, a motion of affection toward the things so known arises naturally in the will. By it the will is drawn and, so to speak, invited to command the intellect to assent to them. God too, as it were, inserts himself into this motion. He flows into it through a particular aid and with that aid as it were sharpens it, so that it presses and draws more strongly, and he makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is fitted for salvation as well.'

sections.title: The free acts of faith and the infused habit
sections.pass_a: CIII. Moreover free choice helped & excited by these two motions of prevenient grace, still has free power of commanding, or not commanding the assent of faith. But if the will wills to embrace the faith, and commands the act of believing to the intellect, the motion of prevenient grace which it has flowing in at the same time, it elicits in itself a supernatural act, by which it wills to embrace the faith, and by which it commands assent to the intellect: and at the same time the intellect moved by that supernatural command of the will, and helped by the divine illustration, elicits a supernatural act of assenting to things revealed, and by these two supernatural acts of intellect & will man duly disposed receives the supernatural habit of faith, infused by God alone, by which thereafter he may be able to produce similar supernatural acts.
pass_b: Thesis CIII. 'Even when these two motions of prevenient grace have helped and roused it, free choice remains free to command the assent of faith or to withhold that command. Suppose the will decides to embrace the faith and orders the intellect to believe. Then, as the motion of prevenient grace it possesses flows in alongside, the will produces within itself a supernatural act: in that act it wills to embrace the faith, and by that act it orders the intellect to assent.

In the same moment the intellect, set in motion by the will's supernatural command and aided by God's light, produces a supernatural act of assent to what God has revealed. A person rightly prepared by these two supernatural acts, one of intellect and one of will, then receives from God alone the infused, supernatural habit of faith, which enables him afterwards to produce further acts of the same supernatural kind.'

sections.title: The motion of grace toward hope
sections.pass_a: CIV. As regards the motion of grace by which we are excited to the act of hope, he explains his mind about it thus. While the intellect, he says, enlightened now by the light of supernatural faith, thinks on the everlasting beatitude prepared for man by God, the goodness and excellence of it, also many other & splendid works of God, and benefits conferred on man, of whose number are Christ's incarnation and passion, and considers the remaining means which have been most abundantly supplied to it for obtaining eternal life, there arises naturally in the will not only an affection toward beatitude, by which it is allured & invited to will it with love of concupiscence, but also a motion of uplift, by which it is drawn & allured to hope for it from God. But although this motion depends on free choice, if it ceases from the thought from which the motion arises; nevertheless, impediments being removed, it rises up merely naturally, and God as it were thrusts himself into it by flowing in specially, and sharpens it & makes it supernatural, that in its order & degree it be such as is necessary to salvation; and through it supernaturally raises up, & as it were invites the will, to elicit the supernatural act of hoping for everlasting beatitude, & the means necessary for obtaining it. Through such grace then our free choice, prevented & excited by God, elicits, if it wills, the first free act of supernatural hope, by which, duly disposed, it obtains from God the habit of supernatural hope, through which hereafter it may elicit other similar supernatural acts as often as it will.
pass_b: Thesis CIV. On the motion of grace that rouses us to the act of hope, he explains his view as follows. 'When the intellect, already enlightened by the light of supernatural faith, thinks about the eternal happiness God has prepared for man, about its goodness and excellence, about God's many other glorious works and the benefits he has conferred on man, among them Christ's incarnation and passion, and considers the other means most abundantly supplied to it for gaining eternal life, there arises naturally in the will not only an affection toward happiness, by which the will is drawn and invited to want it with love of desire, but also a motion of uplift, by which it is attracted and drawn to hope for that happiness from God.

This motion does depend on free choice, if choice turns away from the thought from which the motion arises. Nevertheless, once obstacles are removed, it rises purely by nature, and God, as it were, thrusts himself into it with a special influence. He sharpens it and makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is what salvation requires, and through it he raises the will supernaturally and, so to speak, invites it to elicit the supernatural act of hoping for eternal happiness and for the means needed to gain it.

Through such grace, then, our free choice, anticipated and roused by God, elicits, if it wishes, the first free act of supernatural hope. Duly disposed by that act, it receives from God the habit of supernatural hope, through which it can afterwards elicit other similar supernatural acts whenever it chooses.'

sections.title: The motion of grace toward love of God
sections.pass_a: CV. In agreement with which he also sets out the things concerning the grace necessary for the act of Love of God, & of contrition for sins. Next, he says, when the intellect enlightened by the light of faith, and the act of supernatural hope pre-existing in the will, considers God's goodness both according to itself, and toward us, & so many and great benefits by which he has so sweetly prevented us, there is naturally excited in the will a motion of love of friendship toward God by which that power is allured, & invited to love God. Into this motion too God inserts himself, and by his supernatural influx, not only sharpens & kindles it, but also makes it supernatural, such namely, as in its order & degree is necessary to salvation.
pass_b: Thesis CV. In keeping with this he also discusses the grace needed for the act of love of God and of contrition for sins. 'Next,' he says, 'when the intellect, enlightened by the light of faith, with an act of supernatural hope already present in the will, considers God's goodness both in itself and toward us, and the many great benefits with which he has gone before us so gently, a motion of the love of friendship toward God is stirred up naturally in the will.

By that motion the power is drawn and invited to love God. God inserts himself into this motion too, and by his supernatural influence he not only sharpens and kindles it but also makes it supernatural, of the kind, that is, which in its order and degree is necessary for salvation.'

sections.title: Contrition as the last disposition to sanctifying grace
sections.pass_a: CVI. But if there be added at the same time the knowledge of the magnitude, multitude, and ingratitude of the sins, by which we offend God, free choice prevented by the same grace, as it can elicit the act of supernatural love of God, so will be able to elicit the act of true grief for sins, on account of God loved from the affection of supernatural love, which is true contrition, & the last disposition to sanctifying grace, which in the same instant, but later in nature, follows contrition itself.
pass_b: Thesis CVI. 'If, at the same time, knowledge is added of how great, how many and how ungrateful are the sins by which we offend God, then free choice, anticipated by the same grace, just as it can elicit the act of supernatural love of God, so will be able to elicit the act of true sorrow for sins, felt on account of God, who is loved with an affection of supernatural love.
That sorrow is true contrition and the final disposition for sanctifying grace, which follows contrition in the same instant, though later in the order of nature.'

sections.title: The aid of prevenient grace distinguished from prevenient grace itself
sections.pass_a: CVII. Further that author distinguishes between the aid of prevenient grace, & between prevenient grace itself. And indeed by prevenient grace he understands those cognitions of the mind, & affections of the will, which God by a certain particular influx sharpens & helps, that they become supernatural; & in their degree & order, such as is needful for salvation. But by the aid of prevenient grace he understands that supernatural influx, by which God those cognitions, acquired for the most part by human means, & the affections, rising merely naturally in the will once such cognition is posited, in the way that has been said, sharpens, helps & kindles, that they become supernatural, & such as conduces to the eternal salvation of man.
pass_b: Thesis CVII. Molina also distinguishes the aid of prevenient grace from prevenient grace itself. By prevenient grace he means the knowledge in the mind and the affections in the will that God sharpens and helps by a particular influence so that they become supernatural and, in their degree and order, what salvation requires.

By the aid of prevenient grace he means the supernatural influence by which God sharpens, helps and kindles that knowledge, mostly acquired by human means, and those affections, which, as described, rise purely by nature in the will once such knowledge is present. Through it they become supernatural and of the kind that serves man's eternal salvation.
